## Adversarial Claim Verifier (voter 1/3)

Be SKEPTICAL. Try to REFUTE this claim. ≥2/3 refutations kill it.

## Research question
Research the state of the art in web visual design vocabulary, to extend the reference library of an agent-run pipeline that forges bespoke personal portfolio sites (PIIIX-org/portfolio.me). The pipeline already documents 32 named visual styles across 7 families (surface/material, structural, atmospheric, motion-native, technical/data, textural, reductive) and 72 rendering techniques across 6 groups (GPU/rendering, post-processing, CSS+SVG native, motion/input, whole-page, typographic craft). Its documented GAP is everything about PRESENTING INFORMATION — it has no data-visualization vocabulary and no component-pattern vocabulary at all.

COVER ALL SIX AREAS:

1. DATA AND INFORMATION VISUALIZATION — chart type selection and when each is the right encoding; perceptual ranking of visual encodings (position/length/angle/area/color) and the research behind it; sequential, diverging and categorical color scale construction (including OKLCH/perceptually-uniform approaches and colorblind-safe palettes); small multiples; sparklines and in-line micro-charts; dashboard and stat-tile layout patterns; data storytelling and scrollytelling (scroll-linked chart transitions, annotation layers); editorial data-graphics conventions from newsrooms (NYT, FT, Pudding, Reuters); table design at density (tabular numerals, decimal alignment, hairline rules, sticky headers); how to present evidence and provenance so figures are checkable; accessible charts (screen-reader alternatives, non-color encoding, focus order).

2. COMPONENT AND CONTAINER PATTERNS — cards and their many failure modes; documented ALTERNATIVES to the card grid for presenting a body of projects or work (editorial indexes, tables-as-index, list-with-hover-preview, timelines, maps, filmstrips, stacked/scroll-driven layouts, masonry critiques, single-item-at-a-time patterns, hub-and-spoke); drawers, sheets, side panels, bottom sheets and their platform conventions; modals versus inline expansion versus routed pages, and when each is correct; progressive disclosure patterns; accordions and details/summary; lists — dense, editorial, and interactive; empty, loading and error states as designed deliverables; navigation patterns beyond a top bar.

3. NEW AND EMERGING VISUAL STYLE MOVEMENTS — named aesthetic movements in web and interface design current as of 2025-2026 that are NOT in the list above; include their defining mechanics, their characteristic failure mode, and the condition under which they are the right choice. Also cover which looks now read as generic, templated, or AI-default (so they can be avoided), and the discourse on distinctive versus homogenized web design.

4. MOTION AND INTERACTION FOR THE ABOVE — how cards, drawers, lists and charts should actually behave; shared-element and container transforms; the View Transitions API; disclosure and expansion motion; chart entrance, transition and morphing animation; staggering and orchestration; scroll-linked and scroll-driven reveals; spring/physics versus duration-and-easing, and when each is right.

5. MICRO-INTERACTIONS AND MICRO-ANIMATION — the anatomy and principles of a micro-interaction; feedback, state change and affordance signalling; hover, focus, press and drag states; optimistic UI; haptics; sound; the timing, easing and duration ranges that read as responsive versus sluggish, with the research or platform guidance behind the numbers.

6. LOADING, PROGRESS AND PERCEIVED PERFORMANCE — skeleton screens versus spinners versus progress indicators and the evidence for each; designed preloaders; streaming and progressive rendering; optimistic and predictive loading; perceived-performance research including documented duration thresholds; layout-shift avoidance.

CONSTRAINTS THAT MAKE A FINDING USABLE — prefer and clearly flag findings that satisfy these, and flag ones that violate them:
- Web-native and implementable in HTML/CSS/SVG/canvas/WebGL. Note when a pattern is CSS/SVG-native (cheap) versus requiring a heavy runtime.
- Two-tier budget: a shell under 100KB (HTML, critical CSS, subset fonts, minimal JS) that paints alone with LCP under 1.5s, and a deferred heavy layer. Note byte cost and whether a technique can be deferred.
- Every technique must ship three states: full, a DESIGNED reduced-motion still (never `animation: none`), and a no-WebGL/no-canvas fallback.
- Accessibility is non-negotiable: WCAG contrast, keyboard operability, focus management (especially for drawers, sheets and modals — focus trap, restore, escape, inert background), screen-reader semantics, and non-color encodings.
- Self-hosted and vendored: no CDN in production, no third-party badge or chart services, no hotlinked stock imagery. Visuals are generated (CSS, SVG, canvas, WebGL, procedural) or generated-then-treated in-browser.
- Anti-template: the pipeline's core rule is that two runs must never look alike, so favour findings that support distinctiveness and explicitly name what has become a cliché.

DELIVERABLE — a survey report first: the landscape per area, with concrete named patterns, the mechanics of each, its documented failure mode, the condition under which it is right, and citations. Prefer primary and authoritative sources: peer-reviewed HCI and visualization research, Nielsen Norman Group, MDN and W3C/WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices, platform human-interface guidelines (Apple HIG, Material Design), the published work of newsroom graphics desks, and named practitioners — over listicles and SEO content. Where a number is claimed (a duration threshold, a byte weight, a perceptual ranking), attribute it to its source and note if it is folklore rather than measured. THEN, in a clearly separated final section, map the findings to the repo: which belong as new STYLES.md entries (four-part shape: mechanics / Implies / Fails / Right when), which as new or extended CRAFT.md technique groups (table shape: Technique / What it is / Where it earns its place), and which are new material entirely — flagging any that conflict with the existing rules.

## Claim under review
"Viridis is perceptually uniform and is the current default standard, but it is optimized for normal color vision and NOT for CVD; cividis is the paper's CVD-optimized replacement giving near-identical interpretation for red-green colorblind and non-CVD viewers. So 'we used viridis' is not sufficient evidence of a colorblind-safe sequential scale."

**Source:** https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0199239 (primary)
**Supporting quote:** "Right now, viridis is seen as the gold standard since it follows each of the design principles discussed above; however, it is optimal for those with normal vision and not CVD."

## Checklist
1. Is the claim actually supported by the quote, or is it an overreach/misread?
2. WebSearch for contradicting evidence — does any credible source dispute or heavily qualify this?
3. Is the source quality sufficient for the claim's strength? (extraordinary claims need primary sources)
4. Is the claim outdated? (check dates — old claims about fast-moving fields are suspect)
5. Is this a marketing claim / press release / cherry-picked benchmark / forum speculation?

**refuted=true** if: unsupported by quote / contradicted / low-quality source for strong claim / outdated / marketing fluff.
**refuted=false** ONLY if: claim is well-supported, current, and source quality matches claim strength.
Default to refuted=true if uncertain.

Structured output only. Evidence MUST be specific.

# Ponytail

You are a lazy senior developer. Lazy means efficient, not careless. You have
seen every over-engineered codebase and been paged at 3am for one. The best
code is the code never written.

## Persistence

ACTIVE EVERY RESPONSE. No drift back to over-building. Still active if
unsure. Off only: "stop ponytail" / "normal mode". Default: **full**.
Switch: `/ponytail lite|full|ultra`.

## The ladder

Stop at the first rung that holds:

1. **Does this need to exist at all?** Speculative need = skip it, say so in one line. (YAGNI)
2. **Already in this codebase?** A helper, util, type, or pattern that already lives here → reuse it. Look before you write; re-implementing what's a few files over is the most common slop.
3. **Stdlib does it?** Use it.
4. **Native platform feature covers it?** `<input type="date">` over a picker lib, CSS over JS, DB constraint over app code.
5. **Already-installed dependency solves it?** Use it. Never add a new one for what a few lines can do.
6. **Can it be one line?** One line.
7. **Only then:** the minimum code that works.

The ladder is a reflex, not a research project — but it runs *after* you
understand the problem, not instead of it. Read the task and the code it
touches first, trace the real flow end to end, then climb. Two rungs work →
take the higher one and move on. The first lazy solution that works is the
right one — once you actually know what the change has to touch.

**Bug fix = root cause, not symptom.** A report names a symptom. Before you
edit, grep every caller of the function you're about to touch. The lazy fix IS
the root-cause fix: one guard in the shared function is a smaller diff than a
guard in every caller — and patching only the path the ticket names leaves
every sibling caller still broken. Fix it once, where all callers route through.

## Rules

- No unrequested abstractions: no interface with one implementation, no factory for one product, no config for a value that never changes.
- No boilerplate, no scaffolding "for later", later can scaffold for itself.
- Deletion over addition. Boring over clever, clever is what someone decodes at 3am.
- Fewest files possible. Shortest working diff wins — but only once you understand the problem. The smallest change in the wrong place isn't lazy, it's a second bug.
- Complex request? Ship the lazy version and question it in the same response, "Did X; Y covers it. Need full X? Say so." Never stall on an answer you can default.
- Two stdlib options, same size? Take the one that's correct on edge cases. Lazy means writing less code, not picking the flimsier algorithm.
- Mark deliberate simplifications with a `ponytail:` comment (`// ponytail: this exists`), simple reads as intent, not ignorance. Shortcut with a known ceiling (global lock, O(n²) scan, naive heuristic)? The comment names the ceiling and the upgrade path: `# ponytail: global lock, per-account locks if throughput matters`.

## Output

Code first. Then at most three short lines: what was skipped, when to add it.
No essays, no feature tours, no design notes. If the explanation is longer
than the code, delete the explanation, every paragraph defending a
simplification is complexity smuggled back in as prose. Explanation the user
explicitly asked for (a report, a walkthrough, per-phase notes) is not debt,
give it in full, the rule is only against unrequested prose.

Pattern: `[code] → skipped: [X], add when [Y].`

## Intensity

| Level | What change |
|-------|------------|
| **full** | The ladder enforced. Stdlib and native first. Shortest diff, shortest explanation. Default. |

Example: "Add a cache for these API responses."
- full: "`@lru_cache(maxsize=1000)` on the fetch function. Skipped custom cache class, add when lru_cache measurably falls short."

## When NOT to be lazy

Never simplify away: input validation at trust boundaries, error handling
that prevents data loss, security measures, accessibility basics, anything
explicitly requested. User insists on the full version → build it, no
re-arguing.

Never lazy about understanding the problem. The ladder shortens the
solution, never the reading. Trace the whole thing first — every file the
change touches, the actual flow — before picking a rung. Laziness that skips
comprehension to ship a small diff is the dangerous kind: it dresses up as
efficiency and ships a confident wrong fix. Read fully, then be lazy.

Hardware is never the ideal on paper: a real clock drifts, a real sensor
reads off, a PCA9685 runs a few percent fast. Leave the calibration knob, not
just less code, the physical world needs tuning a minimal model can't see.

Lazy code without its check is unfinished. Non-trivial logic (a branch, a
loop, a parser, a money/security path) leaves ONE runnable check behind, the
smallest thing that fails if the logic breaks: an `assert`-based
`demo()`/`__main__` self-check or one small `test_*.py`. No frameworks, no
fixtures, no per-function suites unless asked. Trivial one-liners need no
test, YAGNI applies to tests too.

## Boundaries

Ponytail governs what you build, not how you talk (pair with Caveman for
terse prose). "stop ponytail" / "normal mode": revert. Level persists until
changed or session end.

The shortest path to done is the right path.
"}}

- _gstack-command: Router for the gstack skill suite. (gstack)
- academic-paper-composer: Systematic writing framework for philosophy and interdisciplinary academic papers from optimized outline to submission-ready manuscript. Use when users want to: (1) write a paper from a detailed outline, (2) ensure quality control during writing, (3) maintain consistency across chapters, (4) prepare a submission-ready manuscript, or (5) systematically execute a planned paper. content.content:
# Analysis of Viridis and Cividis Claims

## On Viridis's Colorblind-Friendliness

The paper states: **"Right now, viridis is seen as the gold standard since it follows each of the design principles discussed above; however, it is optimal for those with normal vision and not CVD."**

Additionally, the authors note that viridis's "CVD-simulated counterpart is close to optimal" but required further improvement through their optimization process.

## On Cividis's Performance

Regarding what cividis achieves across viewer groups, the abstract claims: **"This colormap, cividis, enables nearly-identical visual-data interpretation to both groups, is perceptually uniform in hue and brightness, and increases in brightness linearly."**

## Key Distinction

The paper clearly positions viridis as **not optimized for color vision deficiency**, despite being the current standard. While viridis is described as perceptually uniform and following modern design principles, these principles were not applied with consideration for CVD. Cividis represents their novel contribution: a colormap mathematically optimized for both CVD and non-CVD viewers simultaneously.

Based on the web search results, here's what I found about the viridis colormap:

## Creator and Design

The viridis colormap was created by Stéfan van der Walt and Nathaniel Smith, and it is included in matplotlib. The colormap was merged into the development version of Matplotlib and included in matplotlib 1.5, with viridis becoming the new default colormap in matplotlib 2.0.

## Colorblind-Friendly Design

The colormap is designed to be perfectly perceptually-uniform, both in regular form and when converted to black-and-white, and is also designed to be perceived by readers with the most common form of color blindness.

Regarding the specific types of colorblindness addressed, the most common form of colorblindness is "Moderate deuteranomaly" (a form of deuteranopia), which affects something like 5% of white men.

## Properties

The viridis colormap is designed to improve graph readability for readers with common forms of color blindness and color vision deficiency, and is perceptually-uniform both in regular form and when converted to black-and-white for printing.

An optimized colormap
We used cmaputil to create several example colormaps. We identified one colormap in particular to be optimal for viewing by those with or without CVD, which we name cividis (Figs 4 and
5), generated by optimizing the viridis colormap and selecting the J' linearization that maximizes the range of J'. We chose this map due to its wide range of colors, resulting from a wide
range of J0 values while still changing b0 significantly, and overall sharpness when overlaid
onto complex images. Other optimized colormaps produced using this method had a more
limited J0 range due to spanning more of the b0 space. While spanning more hues is preferable
as well, we felt this colormap had the best balance of hue and lightness range. For the RGB
color values of this colormap, please refer to S2 File. This colormap is also close to optimal for
protanomaly and tritanomaly, as shown in S4 File, where figures are plotted with each of the
forms of CVD with severity set to 100.
Right now, viridis is seen as the gold standard since it follows each of the design principles
discussed above; however, it is optimal for those with normal vision and not CVD. While its
CVD-simulated counterpart is close to optimal, cmaputil helped to further improve upon this
by forcing the perceptual delta to be as close to flat as possible and by increasing the light range
covered. At this time, it is preferable to have both viridis and cividis available to the scientific
community as viridis is more aesthetically pleasing to some and covers more colors for those
with normal vision, allowing greater visual perception sensitivity (Fig 1 viridis CDPS plot vs.
the Fig 5 CDPS plot).
While it may take some time for the full scientific community to both be aware of the need
to choose appropriate colormaps and agree on preferred colormaps, we hope the code we provide here can help with this transition by allowing others to experiment with the different
aspects of colormap design and see how the various characteristics of a colormap affect its
interpretation. Our code can also be leveraged for creating non-monotonically increasing colormaps, by adjusting the J0 linearization function, introducing the ability to create colormaps
for datasets where this is the optimal choice, such as when a diverging colormap is preferred.
Our team has been working to ensure this colormap is easily accessible. As a result, COMSOL [41], the OpenMIMS plugin for ImageJ [42], and Fiji [43], will be adding cividis as an
option among their colormaps. For those who already have a copy of ImageJ, the LUT version
of cividis is provided as S3 File. We will also be reaching out to other software teams to further
increase awareness about our colormap and important considerations in colormap design.
Ideally, we hope to reduce the number of non-perceptually uniform and rainbow-style colormaps being used as default in scientific data analysis software, and to increase the availability
of CVD-friendly colormaps so the estimated more than 600 million individuals worldwide
with CVD can interpret and perceive data like the rest of the population.
An important consideration about our colormap moving forward is it may become obsolete
due to monitors and screens being designed to display larger color gamuts, i.e. colors outside
sRGB colorspace [44, 45]. Our module can again be used for this purpose simply by changing
the sRGB colorspace setting to the more modern colorspace viewed on future screens (e.g., 8K
Ultra HD screens, which may eventually cover nearly twice as much natural color space as the
current sRGB). Additionally, this could better enable cmaputil to create perfectly straight perceptual delta lines, even after conversion to and from CIECAM02-UCS, due to more colors
being available than in sRGB color space.

PLOS ONE | https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0199239 August 1, 2018

10 / 14

 Optimized colormaps for the scientific community

Future work
A downside of cividis, as reported by colleagues, is its minimal coverage of different colors:
varying straight from blue to yellow rather than cycling through other colors, as viridis does.
This keeps cividis from being as aesthetically pleasing as viridis. Of course, this is because
those who have a form of CVD cannot see these colors the way those with normal vision can.
However, since normal color vision is more common, using more colors is often desired for
representation of data and for increasing visual perception precision through use of a larger
dynamic color range. An area of research we are pursuing is the ability to cycle through more
colors while still keeping both normal color vision and deuteranomaly (ranging from a mild
form to complete dichromacy) perceptions of the colormap optimal. Furthermore, by using
CDPS plots (e.g., shown in Figs 1 and 5) to judge our success, we plan to maximize the slope
(m, thus maximizing perceptual sensitivity) while keeping the colormap perceptually uniform
(i.e. r2  1). Viridis is already close to accomplishing this since the perceptual delta of the colormap, as perceived by someone with complete red-green colorblindness, has only a small
imperfection toward the center. Through the next version of cmaputil we hope to create a ªviridis 2.0º, and other aesthetically pleasing colormaps, that are perceptually linear for all people.
It is not clear yet if this task is possible, as those with deuteranomaly but still have trichromatic
vision will be able to see some of the additional colors to varying extents, making it difficult to
optimize for all possible severities. We will try different variations of colormap creation and
optimization to find if this can be done.

input.evidence:
REFUTED as stated — two of its four components are contradicted by the primary source's own text, including the load-bearing final inference.

WHAT SURVIVES (accurate): (a) viridis is perceptually uniform and the de-facto standard — the paper calls it "the gold standard," matplotlib default since 2.0; (b) the quoted sentence "it is optimal for those with normal vision and not CVD" is verbatim; (c) the abstract's cividis claim is verbatim: "This colormap, cividis, enables nearly-identical visual-data interpretation to both groups."

WHAT FAILS:

1. "cividis is the paper's CVD-optimized REPLACEMENT" — directly contradicted, same page. Nuñez/Anderton/Renslow, Discussion: "At this time, it is preferable to have BOTH viridis and cividis available to the scientific community as viridis is more aesthetically pleasing to some and covers more colors for those with normal vision, allowing greater visual perception sensitivity." The paper never asks anyone to stop using viridis. cmaputil's own future-work goal is a "viridis 2.0", i.e. keep viridis's hue range.

2. "'we used viridis' is not sufficient evidence of a colorblind-safe sequential scale" — this is the operational rule and it is an overreach that the same paper undercuts twice. Immediately after the quoted sentence: "While its CVD-simulated counterpart is CLOSE TO OPTIMAL, cmaputil helped to further improve upon this by forcing the perceptual delta to be as close to flat as possible and by increasing the light range covered." And in Future Work: "Viridis is already close to accomplishing this since the perceptual delta of the colormap, AS PERCEIVED BY SOMEONE WITH COMPLETE RED-GREEN COLORBLINDNESS, has only a SMALL IMPERFECTION toward the center." That is the paper certifying viridis as CVD-readable, just not perceptually-uniform-under-CVD. The claim converts "not CVD-OPTIMAL" into "not CVD-SAFE" — a category error. Viridis was explicitly designed for CVD in the first place (van der Walt & Smith; the R package is literally titled "Colorblind-Friendly Color Maps for R", CRAN vignette: designed "to be perceived by viewers with common forms of colour blindness", i.e. moderate deuteranomaly).

3. Independent corroboration of the refutation: Matthew Petroff, "Discernibility of (Rainbow) Colormaps" (2019): "The discernibility of Cividis, which was optimized with color vision deficiencies in mind, is the most consistent between normal color vision and various color vision deficiencies, ALTHOUGH VIRIDIS IS ALSO OKAY IN THIS REGARD, and both are considerably better than any of the rainbow colormaps."

4. Source-strength mismatch for a prescriptive rule: the PLOS ONE paper is a colorimetric-modeling/optimization paper (CIECAM02-UCS deltas + CVD simulation at severity 100). It contains NO human-subject validation, so "near-identical interpretation" is a modeled, not measured, result. A 455-participant heatmap study (arXiv 2506.14775) reports accessibility-optimized maps including Cividis did not close — and sometimes widened — confidence/effort gaps for visually impaired users, so cividis's practical superiority is not empirically settled.

SALVAGEABLE REWRITE for the repo: "Viridis is perceptually uniform AND readable under the common red-green CVDs (it was designed for moderate deuteranomaly); what it is not is perceptually uniform *under CVD simulation* — a CVD viewer gets a slightly compressed reading near the middle of the ramp. Cividis (Nuñez et al. 2018, PLOS ONE) trades hue range for near-identical interpretation across CVD and non-CVD viewers. Pick cividis when cross-group comparability of the *same* figure matters; viridis remains a legitimate colorblind-safe default. Neither is a substitute for a non-color encoding." That version is defensible; the claim as written is not.
